analysis.one_liner: Penalizes drug makers that raise prices faster than inflation and funds Medicare drug-coverage pilot programs with the money.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 26 cosponsors in March 1992, the bill never received a vote in either committee and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut a federal tax credit for pharmaceutical manufacturers whenever they raised prices on brand-name drugs faster than general inflation, and steered the money recovered into a new Medicare outpatient prescription drug trust fund. It would have launched at least 15 five-year demonstration projects testing a Medicare drug benefit, created a Prescription Drug Policy Review Commission to study drug prices here and abroad, and required reports on the federal subsidies the drug industry receives. Medicare did not cover outpatient prescription drugs at the time, and the bill's own findings said drug prices were rising three times faster than general inflation.
analysis.who_benefits: Elderly and other patients who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs, especially Medicare beneficiaries with no drug coverage — the bill's findings said prescription drugs were the highest out-of-pocket medical cost for three of four elderly patients. Community health centers and pharmacists would also have gained from the demonstration projects' funding and reimbursement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors paying out of pocket for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the Puerto Rico and possessions tax credit (section 936) for manufacturers of brand-name drugs whose prices rise faster than the Consumer Price Index, with a formula that scales the penalty to how much each drug's price increase exceeds inflation [S2] [S3].

Creates a Medicare Outpatient Prescription Drug Trust Fund financed by the recovered tax credit, funding at least 15 five-year demonstration projects testing a Medicare outpatient drug benefit and extended drug coverage at community health centers [S2] [S3].

Establishes a Prescription Drug Policy Review Commission to report annually on drug price trends, including international comparisons, and to study the feasibility of a US pharmaceutical price review board like those used in Canada and other industrialized nations [S2] [S3].

Requires a report on the total cost to taxpayers of all federal subsidies to the pharmaceutical industry, and a determination of how tax credits and market exclusivity could be tied to manufacturers' pricing behavior [S2] [S3].
Requires manufacturers to report the average prices they charge for drugs in Canada, Australia, and European Community countries, giving the US government data on foreign drug prices [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, through a reduced section 936 tax credit — the bill's findings cited over $1.4 billion in such credits to the industry in 1987 and an estimated $2 billion in 1990. Puerto Rico's drug-manufacturing sector, whose tax advantage would shrink, would bear part of the cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill's centerpiece is a penalty formula that claws back a tax credit when prices rise too fast; it pressures prices indirectly rather than capping or negotiating them, so drug makers could simply accept the credit reduction and keep raising prices.

The Medicare drug benefit is only a set of demonstration projects in selected areas, not a national benefit; beneficiaries outside the project areas would get no new coverage, and the full results were not due until five years after enactment.
Shrinking the section 936 credit could reduce the tax advantage that draws pharmaceutical manufacturing to Puerto Rico, with potential job losses on the island.

The bill leans heavily on new commissions, studies, and reports — a Prescription Drug Policy Review Commission, a feasibility study of a price review board, a subsidies report, and international price data — deferring any direct price control decision to a later Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct help to patients would have been modest at first — the trust fund's project funding was set at roughly $200 million a year, concentrated in demonstration areas — while the pricing pressure on manufacturers applied nationally and permanently. The tradeoff is a real one: genuine but partial relief for seniors and a long-term check on drug-price inflation, in exchange for a slower, study-heavy approach and some risk to Puerto Rico manufacturing employment.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and their health subcommittees in March 1992, neither committee ever took it up, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Byron Dorgan of North Dakota introduced the Prescription Drug Cost Containment Act of 1992 on March 18, 1992, with nine original cosponsors including Nancy Pelosi, Dick Durbin, and Les Aspin [S3] [S5].
The bill was referred jointly to the House Committees on Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced [S1] [S5].
Within two weeks it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health (Ways and Means) and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment (Energy and Commerce) — the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
Twenty-five members cosponsored the bill: 23 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent [S4].
No committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever held, and the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: they kept the section 936 tax credit — worth over $1.4 billion to the industry in 1987 by the bill's own findings — and faced no penalty mechanism for raising prices faster than inflation. Seniors without drug coverage got no Medicare benefit, pilot or otherwise.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was mostly Democratic — 23 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent out of 435 House members — but no vote was ever taken, so the chambers' actual partisan split never showed.

industries.note: The bill would have reduced their section 936 possessions tax credit — which the bill's findings valued at over $1.4 billion in 1987 — whenever their prices rose faster than inflation, tying the size of the penalty directly to their price increases. The industry's interest in blocking the bill was preserving that credit and its pricing freedom, which ordinary patients pay for at the pharmacy.

The tax credit the bill targets exists to encourage US manufacturing in Puerto Rico; drug makers on the island would have seen the credit's value shrink relative to wages paid there. That could cost island jobs, though the bill preserved a wage-based portion of the credit.
The bill would have funded demonstration projects extending outpatient prescription drug coverage to Medicare beneficiaries served by community health centers, using the recovered tax revenue.
At least five demonstration projects would have separately reimbursed pharmacists for medication regimen review and drug utilization management services, and paid dispensing at marketplace rates.
